analysis.investment_thesis: Prodocs fails the Magic Formula on both axes — an earnings yield of roughly 3.9% (P/E 25.5) is expensive, and an ROE of 0.41% signals near-zero return on capital. You cannot buy a cheap-and-good business here; it is neither cheap nor good.
key_strengths: Asset-light non-voice BPO model typically needs low capex
Small FII presence (3.70%) suggests some institutional screening
key_risks: ROE of 0.41% implies effectively no return on invested capital
P/E 25.5 = earnings yield ~3.9%, well below the >12% Magic Formula threshold
Tiny Rs 130 Cr micro-cap in commoditized ITES with no visible moat
red_flags: Return on capital far below 12% minimum
Earnings yield under 6% — overvalued on Magic Formula basis
Incorporated 2019 — no 3-year sustained ROIC track record
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula ranks companies on two factors: earnings yield (EBIT/EV) and return on capital. Prodocs scores poorly on both. A P/E of 25.5 translates to an earnings yield of roughly 3.9% — you need >12% for this to be interesting. More damning, an ROE of 0.41% means the business is barely earning anything on its equity base; this is the opposite of the high-ROIC compounder the formula is designed to surface. Non-voice BPO is a commodity service with low switching costs, so a structural re-rating of returns is unlikely.

At Rs 130 Cr market cap with these metrics, you are paying a growth-stock multiple for a no-growth-in-returns business. The systematic approach — which exists precisely to remove emotional bias — would never surface this name. I would pass and redeploy capital to companies that rank in the top decile on both cheapness and quality. No bet here.
